desk.name: Electrochemistry — Electrolysis & Electrolytes
desk.description: Select any 2 solutions/substances to explore electrochemistry — conductivity tests, electrolysis products at cathode and anode, colour changes, gas evolution, metal deposition, and electroplating.
desk.mode_note: In this desk, one chemical acts as the ELECTROLYTE (solution in the cell) and the second acts as the ELECTRODE MATERIAL or REAGENT. The experiment always uses a DC power supply connected to two electrodes dipped into the electrolyte.

chemicals.name: Silver Nitrate Solution
chemicals.hazard: oxidising — stains skin black; avoid contact

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate — Inert (Graphite) Electrodes

output.color_fade_note: Blue colour fades as Cu2+ ions are removed from solution
output.observation: Pink-brown copper metal deposits on the cathode (negative electrode). Colourless oxygen gas bubbles form at the anode. The blue colour of the solution slowly fades as Cu2+ ions are used up.

reactions.educational_note: Cu2+ ions are reduced at the cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. OH- ions are oxidised at the anode releasing O2. This is reduction at cathode and oxidation at anode — a redox process. The fading blue colour confirms Cu2+ ions are being removed.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate — Active Copper Electrodes (Copper Purification)
reactions.formula: Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu | Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-

output.color_change_note: Blue colour stays constant — Cu2+ replenished as fast as it is used
output.observation: Copper deposits on the cathode — it grows heavier. The anode slowly dissolves — it grows lighter. The blue colour of the solution stays constant throughout!

reactions.educational_note: With copper electrodes, the anode dissolves (Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-) and copper deposits at cathode (Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu). The Cu2+ concentration stays constant — so the blue colour does NOT fade. This principle is used industrially to purify copper.

reactions.name: Copper Sulfate Solution + Zinc Electrode — Displacement (No Electrolysis)

output.observation: Without any electricity — just by placing zinc into copper sulfate — a reddish-brown copper coating appears on the zinc. The blue colour fades. This is a spontaneous displacement, not electrolysis!

reactions.educational_note: Zinc is higher than copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper spontaneously: Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu. No electricity needed! The blue colour fades as Cu2+ is removed. This contrasts beautifully with electrolysis — same result, different method.

reactions.name: Copper Sulfate + Silver Nitrate — Two Electrolytes Mixed

output.observation: When mixed, a faint white precipitate of silver sulfate may form. Both are electrolytes, so the mixture still conducts well. No electrolysis reaction occurs without a power supply.

reactions.educational_note: Both CuSO4 and AgNO3 are strong electrolytes. When mixed without power, SO42- and Ag+ can form a slight white precipitate of Ag2SO4. To electrolyse this mixture, a DC power supply would be needed.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Brine (NaCl) — Graphite Electrodes

output.anode_gas_test: bleaches moist litmus paper — turns white
output.observation: Colourless hydrogen gas (squeaky pop) bubbles at the cathode. Yellow-green chlorine gas (bleaches litmus) bubbles at the anode. The remaining solution becomes alkaline (NaOH).

reactions.educational_note: The electrolysis of brine is industrially vital — it produces three useful products: H2 (fuel), Cl2 (disinfectant/bleach), and NaOH (used in soap making). At the cathode, H+ ions are discharged in preference to Na+ (Na is too reactive). At the anode, Cl- ions are discharged in preference to OH- when concentration is high.

reactions.name: NaCl Solution + Copper Electrode — Copper Dissolves, No NaCl Electrolysis
reactions.formula: Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e- | Cathode: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2 (or Na+ stays)

output.anode_product: copper electrode dissolves — Cu2+ ions enter solution
output.color_change_note: Solution gradually turns light blue as Cu2+ ions dissolve from copper anode
output.observation: Hydrogen gas bubbles at the cathode with a squeaky pop. The copper anode slowly dissolves, turning the colourless salt solution light blue as Cu2+ ions enter it.

reactions.educational_note: When a copper electrode is used as the anode, it dissolves preferentially — even in NaCl solution. Active anodes are oxidised instead of the solution's anions. The solution turns blue, showing Cu2+ is entering it.

reactions.name: NaCl Solution + Zinc Electrode — Zinc Anode Dissolves

output.observation: Hydrogen gas (squeaky pop) forms at the cathode. The zinc anode slowly corrodes and becomes lighter. The solution remains colourless as Zn2+ is colourless.

reactions.educational_note: Active electrodes (zinc here) dissolve at the anode during electrolysis. Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-. At cathode, H+ from water is reduced to H2 since Na+ is too reactive. This is similar in principle to the zinc-copper galvanic cell.

reactions.name: Brine + Silver Nitrate — AgCl White Precipitate Forms

output.observation: A curdy white precipitate of silver chloride instantly forms when silver nitrate is added to brine. This is the classic halide ion test — confirms chloride ions are present in the solution.

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO3. The white precipitate of AgCl is the standard test for Cl- ions (halide test). AgCl is insoluble — even though both reactants dissolved easily. This is not an electrolysis reaction — it is an ionic precipitation.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Dilute H2SO4 — Acidified Water

output.observation: Vigorous bubbling at both electrodes. Hydrogen (2 volumes) at cathode — squeaky pop. Oxygen (1 volume) at anode — relights glowing splint. Volume ratio 2:1 confirms water composition (H2O).

reactions.educational_note: Electrolysis of acidified water decomposes water into H2 and O2. The ratio 2:1 (H2:O2) matches the formula H2O — 2 hydrogens to 1 oxygen. H2SO4 is only a conductor — it is not decomposed. This is how water's composition was first proved experimentally.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Copper Electrode — Copper Anode Dissolves

output.color_change_note: Solution turns blue as Cu2+ ions dissolve from copper anode
output.observation: Hydrogen bubbles at the cathode. The copper anode dissolves slowly, turning the colourless acid solution blue as Cu2+ ions are released. The solution gains a noticeable blue tint over time.

reactions.educational_note: Active copper anode dissolves in preference to SO42- or OH- oxidation. Cu → Cu2+ + 2e- at anode; 2H+ + 2e- → H2 at cathode. The solution turning blue is a clear visual indicator of Cu2+ production.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Zinc Electrode — Zinc Dissolves, H2 Produced (Without Electricity)
reactions.formula: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 (spontaneous acid-metal reaction)

output.observation: No power supply needed! Zinc reacts spontaneously with sulfuric acid — vigorous fizzing with colourless hydrogen gas (squeaky pop). The zinc metal gradually dissolves. This is a metal-acid reaction, NOT electrolysis.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2↑. Zinc reacts with dilute acid without any electricity — it is a simple displacement reaction. This contrasts with electrolysis where an external power supply forces the decomposition. Hydrogen test: burning splint produces a squeaky pop.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Silver Nitrate — No Precipitate (Both Ionic, Compatible)
reactions.formula: H2SO4 + AgNO3 -> Ag2SO4 (slight white precipitate) + HNO3

output.observation: A faint white precipitate of silver sulfate forms when silver nitrate is added to sulfuric acid. Both solutions are highly conductive electrolytes. No gas produced without a power supply.

reactions.educational_note: H2SO4 + 2AgNO3 → Ag2SO4↓ + 2HNO3. Silver sulfate is sparingly soluble — giving a faint precipitate. This shows that electrolyte solutions can still react chemically even without electricity — through ionic precipitation.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Dilute HCl — H2 at Cathode, Cl2 at Anode

output.anode_gas_test: bleaches moist litmus paper — turns white
output.observation: Hydrogen (squeaky pop) bubbles at the cathode. Pale yellow-green chlorine gas (bleaches moist litmus) forms at the anode. Same products as brine but solution is acidic throughout.

reactions.educational_note: HCl fully dissociates: HCl → H+ + Cl-. At cathode: H+ reduced to H2. At anode: Cl- oxidised to Cl2. Unlike NaCl (brine), no NaOH byproduct forms. The chlorine gas test — moist litmus bleached white — is a key school test.

reactions.name: HCl + Copper Electrode — Copper Dissolves, H2 at Cathode

output.color_change_note: Solution turns blue-green as Cu2+ ions enter from dissolving copper anode
output.observation: Hydrogen gas (squeaky pop) at cathode. The copper anode dissolves, and the colourless acid gradually turns blue-green (Cu2+ ions in solution). Two dramatic changes — gas AND colour!

reactions.educational_note: Copper anode dissolves preferentially over Cl- oxidation: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-. Cu2+ in solution gives the characteristic blue-green colour. The H+ at cathode is reduced to H2. This is a visually rich electrolysis experiment.

reactions.name: HCl + Zinc — Spontaneous Reaction (Acid + Metal, No Electricity)

output.observation: Vigorous fizzing immediately — no electricity needed! Zinc dissolves as it reacts with hydrochloric acid. Colourless hydrogen gas with a squeaky pop is produced. This is a straightforward metal + acid reaction.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2↑. Zinc is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen from acid spontaneously. No power supply needed. Students should learn to distinguish spontaneous chemical reactions from forced electrolysis.

reactions.name: HCl + Silver Nitrate — White Precipitate of AgCl (Halide Test)

output.precipitate_solubility_test: insoluble in HNO3 — confirms Cl- ion
output.observation: An immediate curdy white precipitate of AgCl forms. This is the classic test for chloride ions. The precipitate is insoluble in dilute nitric acid — this confirms it is AgCl (not AgBr or AgI).

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 + HCl → AgCl↓ + HNO3. AgCl is a curdy white precipitate — insoluble in dilute HNO3. This is the standard school test for Cl- (halide ion test). AgBr gives pale cream; AgI gives yellow. Insolubility in HNO3 confirms chloride.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of NaOH Solution — Water Decomposed to H2 + O2

output.observation: Vigorous gas at both electrodes. Twice as much hydrogen (cathode) as oxygen (anode). Hydrogen: squeaky pop. Oxygen: relights glowing splint. NaOH acts as conductor, not decomposed.

reactions.educational_note: NaOH provides ions (Na+, OH-) making the solution a good conductor, but water is electrolysed — not NaOH. Na+ is too reactive to be discharged at cathode — H2O is reduced instead. The 2:1 ratio of H2:O2 is the key result proving H2O composition.

reactions.name: NaOH Solution + Copper Electrode — Copper Anode Dissolves
reactions.formula: Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e- | Cu2+ + 2OH- -> Cu(OH)2 (blue precipitate)

output.anode_product: copper electrode dissolves; Cu(OH)2 blue precipitate forms
output.precipitate_name: Copper Hydroxide Cu(OH)2 — pale blue gelatinous precipitate
output.observation: Hydrogen gas at cathode. Copper anode dissolves releasing Cu2+ ions. These immediately react with OH- in NaOH solution to form pale blue copper hydroxide precipitate. A dramatic double change — gas AND precipitate!

reactions.educational_note: Cu2+ from the dissolving anode reacts with OH- in NaOH: Cu2+ + 2OH- → Cu(OH)2 (blue precipitate). This is a double observation — active electrode behaviour + precipitation. Shows the interaction between electrode material and electrolyte.

reactions.name: NaOH Solution + Zinc Electrode — Zinc Dissolves in Alkali
reactions.formula: Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2 (spontaneous — zinc is amphoteric)

output.observation: Zinc slowly dissolves in NaOH solution producing hydrogen gas — even without electricity! This is unusual because zinc reacts with both acids AND alkalis. Gentle bubbling, squeaky pop confirms H2.

reactions.educational_note: Zinc is amphoteric — it reacts with both acids and alkalis. Zn + 2NaOH → Na2ZnO2 + H2↑ (sodium zincate). This spontaneous reaction demonstrates amphoteric behaviour — an important Grade 10 concept.

reactions.name: NaOH + Silver Nitrate — Brown/Black Silver Oxide Precipitate

output.observation: A dark brown/black precipitate of silver oxide instantly forms. The mixture turns muddy brown. Silver nitrate + alkali is a dramatic reaction — the precipitate is very dark and insoluble.

reactions.educational_note: 2AgNO3 + 2NaOH → Ag2O↓ + 2NaNO3 + H2O. Silver oxide is the dark brown/black precipitate. This reaction is used in qualitative analysis to confirm Ag+ ions. Contrasts with AgCl (white) from Cl- test.

reactions.name: Glucose Solution — Non-Electrolyte, No Conduction

output.observation: The bulb does NOT light up. No bubbles at either electrode. Glucose dissolves in water but does NOT form ions — it is a non-electrolyte and cannot conduct electricity.

reactions.educational_note: Glucose (C6H12O6) is a molecular (covalent) compound. It dissolves in water but does NOT dissociate into ions. No ions = no current = no electrolysis. This is the key difference between electrolytes (ionic) and non-electrolytes (molecular).

reactions.name: Glucose Solution + Copper Electrode — No Reaction
reactions.formula: C6H12O6 (aq) + Cu — no conduction, no electrolysis

output.observation: The bulb stays off. No reaction at copper electrodes. Glucose is a non-electrolyte — no ions means no current, no electrolysis, and no electrode reactions.

reactions.educational_note: Even with a reactive metal electrode, if the solution is a non-electrolyte, no current can flow and no electrolysis occurs. Both an ionic electrolyte AND a complete circuit are required.

reactions.name: Glucose Solution + Zinc — No Reaction

output.observation: No reaction at all. Zinc does not react with glucose solution (unlike with acids or alkalis). No gas, no colour change, no current flow — glucose is a non-electrolyte.

reactions.educational_note: Zinc reacts with acids (H+) and alkalis (OH-) but not with neutral non-electrolytes like glucose. No ions means no driving force for a chemical or electrochemical reaction.

reactions.name: Glucose + Silver Nitrate — Tollens'-like Silver Mirror Reaction
reactions.formula: C6H12O6 + 2Ag+ -> C6H12O7 + 2Ag (silver mirror — with ammonia and heat)

output.precipitate_name: Silver metal — shiny mirror on glass wall
output.observation: When heated gently with silver nitrate (and ammonia), glucose acts as a reducing agent — silver ions are reduced to shiny silver metal forming a mirror on the glass wall. This shows glucose is a reducing sugar.

reactions.educational_note: Glucose is a reducing sugar — it donates electrons to Ag+ reducing it to Ag metal (the silver mirror test / Tollens' test). This shows glucose can participate in redox reactions even though it is a non-electrolyte. It does NOT conduct electricity, but it CAN reduce metal ions chemically.

reactions.name: Distilled Water — Very Poor Conductor, Almost No Electrolysis

output.observation: The bulb does NOT light up — or shows only the faintest glow. No visible gas at electrodes. Pure water is an extremely poor conductor because it has almost no free ions.

reactions.educational_note: Pure water has an extremely low ion concentration (Kw = 10-14). It is effectively a non-conductor. This is why tap water conducts (dissolved minerals) but distilled water does not. Adding an electrolyte like H2SO4 dramatically increases conductivity.

reactions.name: Distilled Water + Copper Electrode — No Electrolysis
reactions.formula: H2O + Cu electrode — negligible current, no useful electrolysis

output.observation: No visible reaction. Distilled water has no ions, so even copper electrodes cannot drive any useful electrolysis. The bulb stays off completely.

reactions.educational_note: Even a reactive active electrode cannot compensate for the absence of charge carriers (ions). Distilled water + copper electrodes = no circuit completion, no electrolysis.

reactions.name: Distilled Water + Zinc — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Zn + H2O -> no reaction at room temperature

output.observation: No reaction. Zinc does not react with distilled water at room temperature. No bubbles, no colour change. Zinc only reacts with steam at high temperatures.

reactions.educational_note: Zinc + water → no reaction at room temperature (unlike very reactive metals such as sodium or potassium). Zinc needs steam (very high temperature) or an acid/alkali to react. This is a useful reminder of the reactivity series.

reactions.name: Distilled Water + Silver Nitrate — AgNO3 Dissolves Easily

output.observation: Silver nitrate dissolves completely and instantly in distilled water to give a clear, colourless solution. The solution now conducts electricity — the bulb lights up. AgNO3 is a strong electrolyte.

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 is an ionic compound — it fully dissociates: AgNO3 → Ag+ + NO3-. These free ions carry the current. This experiment beautifully contrasts distilled water (no conduction) with AgNO3 solution (bright bulb) — showing that ions are essential for conductivity.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Copper Chloride — Cu Deposit + Cl2 Gas

output.color_fade_note: Blue-green colour fades as Cu2+ and Cl- ions are removed
output.observation: Pink-brown copper deposits on the cathode. Pale yellow-green chlorine gas (bleaches moist litmus) bubbles at the anode. The blue-green solution gradually fades as BOTH Cu2+ and Cl- ions are removed.

reactions.educational_note: CuCl2 → Cu2+ + 2Cl-. At cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (pink deposit). At anode: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e- (yellow-green gas bleaches litmus). The solution fades as BOTH ions are removed — unlike CuSO4 where only Cu2+ is removed.

reactions.name: CuCl2 + Copper Electrodes — Copper Transfer (Electroplating)
reactions.formula: Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu | Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-

output.color_change_note: Colour stays constant — Cu2+ consumed and replenished equally
output.observation: Copper deposits on cathode; copper anode slowly dissolves. The blue-green colour stays constant — confirming Cu2+ is continuously replenished. This is the electroplating principle: coating objects with copper.

reactions.educational_note: With active copper electrodes in CuCl2: the cathode gains copper; the anode loses copper. [Cu2+] stays constant. This is the basis of electroplating — useful for coating jewellery, circuit boards, and industrial parts with a layer of copper.

reactions.name: CuCl2 + Zinc Electrode — Displacement Without Electricity

output.observation: No electricity needed! Zinc placed into copper chloride solution immediately gets coated in reddish-brown copper. The blue-green colour fades. Zinc is more reactive than copper — it spontaneously displaces it.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + CuCl2 → ZnCl2 + Cu. Zinc displaces copper spontaneously — no power supply needed. The reactivity series predicts this: Zn > Cu. This is a galvanic (spontaneous) reaction, contrasted with forced electrolysis.

reactions.name: CuCl2 + Silver Nitrate — White AgCl AND Blue Cu2+ Persist

output.precipitate_name: Silver Chloride (AgCl) — curdy white precipitate in blue-green solution
output.observation: A white precipitate of AgCl forms instantly. But the solution remains blue-green — because Cu2+ ions do NOT precipitate with NO3-. You can see white flakes in a blue-green liquid — a striking contrast.

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 precipitates Cl- as AgCl (white). But Cu(NO3)2 stays in solution — blue-green. This elegant result shows selective precipitation: Cl- is removed but Cu2+ stays. Confirms Cl- presence (halide test) even in a blue-green electrolyte.

reactions.name: Graphite Electrode + Copper Electrode — Galvanic Cell Setup
reactions.formula: Graphite (cathode) + Cu (anode) in electrolyte -> small voltage generated

output.bulb_brightness: none — needs electrolyte to complete circuit
output.observation: Two solid electrodes placed together without a solution produce no reaction and no voltage. An electrolyte solution is needed to complete the circuit. This setup alone is incomplete.

reactions.educational_note: Electrodes alone do nothing — a complete electrochemical circuit requires: two electrodes + an electrolyte solution + connecting wires + a DC source (for electrolysis) OR a spontaneous redox driving force (for galvanic cells). No electrolyte = open circuit.

reactions.name: Graphite + Zinc — Zinc-Carbon Galvanic Cell (Dry Cell Concept)
reactions.formula: Anode: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e- | Cathode: (reduction at graphite) — needs electrolyte

output.observation: Graphite and zinc electrodes alone do nothing. But this is the exact same combination as an everyday dry cell (AA battery)! In a battery, the electrolyte (ammonium chloride paste) connects them. Without it — no current.

reactions.educational_note: A zinc-carbon dry cell (AA battery) uses graphite (positive/cathode) and zinc (negative/anode) with ammonium chloride paste as electrolyte. Without the electrolyte, no circuit is complete and no current flows. This pair shows the importance of the electrolyte in any cell.

reactions.name: Graphite Electrode + Silver Nitrate — Electroplating with Silver
reactions.formula: Cathode (graphite): Ag+ + e- -> Ag | Anode: needs silver or inert anode

output.cathode_product: shiny silver metal deposits on graphite cathode
output.anode_product: O2 gas if inert anode used
output.observation: With DC power, shiny silver metal deposits on the graphite cathode — it turns silvery! Ag+ ions from the silver nitrate solution are reduced to Ag metal. This is the principle of silver electroplating.

reactions.educational_note: Silver electroplating: Ag+ + e- → Ag at cathode. The graphite acts as the object to be plated. Industrially, jewellery and cutlery are silver-plated this way using AgNO3 as electrolyte and a silver anode. This demonstrates a real-world electrochemistry application.

reactions.name: Copper + Zinc Electrodes — Galvanic Cell (Simple Battery)
reactions.formula: Anode: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e- | Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu | EMF ~1.1V

output.observation: When connected in an electrolyte, the voltmeter deflects — a voltage is produced! Zinc is the negative terminal (anode); copper is the positive terminal (cathode). This is a simple galvanic cell — a battery! No power supply needed.

reactions.educational_note: Zn-Cu in electrolyte = a galvanic (voltaic) cell. Zn loses electrons (oxidised at anode); Cu2+ gains electrons (reduced at cathode). EMF ≈ 1.1V. This is the Daniell cell — the first practical battery. Shows spontaneous redox reactions produce electricity.

reactions.name: Copper + Silver Nitrate — Copper Displaces Silver (No Electricity)

output.precipitate_name: Silver metal — feathery/spiky silver crystals on copper surface
output.observation: No electricity needed! Feathery silver crystals grow on the copper surface. The colourless solution slowly turns blue as Cu2+ ions enter. Copper is displacing silver — stunning to observe!

reactions.educational_note: Cu + 2Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2Ag. Copper is above silver in the reactivity series — it displaces silver spontaneously. The beautiful dendritic silver crystals and the blue Cu2+ colour change make this a visually dramatic experiment. No electricity needed — it is a galvanic/spontaneous redox reaction.

reactions.name: Zinc + Silver Nitrate — Zinc Displaces Silver

output.precipitate_name: Silver metal — grey metallic precipitate on zinc
output.observation: Silver metal deposits on the zinc surface — no electricity needed! Zinc is higher than silver in the reactivity series, so it displaces silver rapidly. Grey metallic sheen appears on the zinc. Faster than Cu + AgNO3.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + 2AgNO3 → Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag. Zinc is more reactive than silver — displaces it spontaneously. No power needed. Zn(NO3)2 is colourless, so no colour change in the solution (unlike Cu + AgNO3 which turns blue). Reactivity series: Zn > Cu > Ag.
